sources.title: Occupation and Reconstruction of Japan, 1945-52
sources.note: three phases of occupation; peace treaty and U.S. bases. Scope: U.S. diplomatic framing; pair with Japanese and Okinawan sources and do not treat occupation policy as social outcome.

sources.title: The Constitution of Japan (official English presentation)
sources.note: Preamble; Articles 9, 14, 24, 25, 26. Scope: Constitutional guarantees do not by themselves prove immediate implementation or equal lived access.

sources.title: 日本国憲法 (official Japanese text)
sources.note: 第二十四条, first sentence. Scope: Current legal database presentation of a 1946 text; quotation is statutory text, not manuscript facsimile.

sources.title: Birth of the Constitution chronological table, October 1945-January 1946
sources.note: December 17, 1945 election-law revision; women gain the vote. Scope: Legal enfranchisement did not end gender hierarchy or guarantee equal political power.

sources.title: Main Issues: Guarantees for Fundamental Human Rights
sources.note: discussion of GHQ draft and negotiations over social rights. Scope: Use to explain drafting, not to reduce the constitution to a unilateral American gift.

sources.title: GHQ/SCAP censorship marks on postwar correspondence
sources.note: Trivia: Censorship by GHQ/SCAP; September 1945-October 1949. Scope: The page gives examples and institutional scope; it does not quantify every censored item or effect.

sources.title: Surrender of Japan (Instrument of Surrender)
sources.note: full transcript, especially paragraphs 1, 2, and 8. Scope: Formal surrender did not erase Japanese institutions or mean direct American rule of every locality.

sources.title: Treaty of Peace with Japan, UNTS No. 1832
sources.note: entry into force; Articles 2, 3, 23. Scope: Treaty language generated enduring territorial disputes; report text and administration without pretending all sovereignty questions were settled.

sources.title: Treaty of Mutual Cooperation and Security between Japan and the United States
sources.note: Articles V, VI, IX and signatures. Scope: Treaty text does not itself explain the mass Anpo protests or unequal local burdens.

sources.title: Major events in postwar Okinawa
sources.note: 1945 Nimitz Proclamation, Okinawa Advisory Council, 1952 Government of the Ryukyus. Scope: Okinawa is outside the atlas polygon; include as contrast, never as evidence that the main-island polygon remained occupied after 1952.

sources.title: Military land acquisition across Okinawa, 1941-1972
sources.note: sections 1945-1952 and 1952-1972; land-title confirmation and island-wide protest. Scope: Out-of-polygon contrast; do not generalize Okinawa's base burden to all Japan.

sources.title: Okinawa's postwar history exhibit
sources.note: Exhibition Room 5: refugee camps, 27-year occupation, reversion movement. Scope: Museum overview should be supplemented with named testimonies for individual experience.

sources.title: Ainu History and Culture
sources.note: incorporation into Japan; 1899 law; discrimination and cultural transmission. Scope: Broad chronology; avoid attributing identical experience to all Ainu communities in the target interval.

sources.title: National Ainu Museum permanent exhibition
sources.note: Our Language, Our Lives, Our History, Our Work, Our Exchange. Scope: Continuity exhibit is not proof that every displayed practice was unchanged or universally practiced in 1945-1960.

sources.title: Transition of Ainu Culture After World War II
sources.note: 1945-1973 'culture preservation measures' period and discrimination. Scope: Abstract-level evidence is broad; check the Japanese full text before using detailed local examples.

sources.title: Japan Statistical Yearbook: Population and prefectures, 1920-2021
sources.note: Tables 2-1 and 2-3; 1945, 1950, 1955, 1960; Okinawa and Amami footnotes. Scope: Definitions and territorial coverage change; never compare figures without printing the footnotes.

sources.title: Historical population and vital statistics tables
sources.note: birth, death, natural increase, infant mortality for 1947, 1950, 1955, 1960. Scope: National aggregates conceal class, rural/urban, Ainu, Okinawan, and pollution-region inequality.

sources.title: Fiscal and Monetary Policies of Japan in Reconstruction and High-Growth, 1945-1971
sources.note: Part 1, chapters 1-3: postwar inflation, Dodge Plan, land reform, post-treaty policy. Scope: Macroeconomic policy cannot stand in for household hardship or unequal labor outcomes.

sources.title: The Livelihood Improvement Approach
sources.note: rural women's groups; improved kamado stoves; sanitation and household problem-solving. Scope: Program retrospective can overstate coherence and success; describe examples, not a universal rural transformation.

sources.title: Housing reconstruction in war-damaged cities in the late 1940s
sources.note: pp. 191-212; noncommercial housing creation and distribution. Scope: Urban regulatory history; do not generalize to rural homes or all bombed cities.

sources.title: National Showa Memorial Museum permanent exhibition
sources.note: Departing from the ruins; children's postwar years; toward recovery; 1955-1964 experience area. Scope: Exhibit reconstruction and nostalgia need object-level citations; not every display represents every household.

sources.title: National Museum of Japanese History Gallery 6: Contemporary Japan
sources.note: postwar black-market reconstruction; 'postwar lifestyle revolution'; dam-submerged village. Scope: Gallery narratives span beyond 1960; isolate objects and events within the target interval.

sources.title: The Enactment of the School Education Law
sources.note: March 31-April 1, 1947; 6-3-3-4 system. Scope: Legal structure does not prove equal facilities, attendance, or outcomes in every locality.

sources.title: Physical Education and Athletics: postwar school health and lunch programs
sources.note: school lunches resumed in 1947; 1950 eight cities; 1951 program scale; 1946 National Athletic Meet. Scope: Government program reach changed rapidly; avoid implying every child received the same lunch.

sources.title: Implementation of the new educational system and Courses of Study
sources.note: 1947 tentative curricula; social studies, homemaking, free study. Scope: Curriculum plans are not classroom ethnography; teacher practice and resources varied.

sources.title: Postwar Reconstruction of Education and Further Development, 1945-c.1960
sources.note: Section 4, postwar reconstruction 1945-c.1960. Scope: Modernization narrative can emphasize institutional success; pair with shortage and inequality evidence.

sources.title: How did Japanese rural dwellers become rapidly healthier after World War II?
sources.note: pp. 123-132; health, livelihood, agriculture, social education interventions. Scope: Review advances a multicausal hypothesis; do not turn association into a precise causal share.

sources.title: Development of public health administration in postwar Japan
sources.note: pp. 113-147; 1945 memorandum, health centers, infectious disease. Scope: Institutional history; services and access differed by region and population.

sources.title: Postwar Japanese movement for a life without mosquitoes and flies
sources.note: community organization, pest control, resident participation. Scope: Program study does not demonstrate universal participation or eradication.

sources.title: Disease, Environment, and Causation: reform toilets in modern Japan
sources.note: discussion of kairyō-benjo and continuation after 1945. Scope: Do not infer one national toilet type; verify target-period pages and regional examples before detailed wording.

sources.title: Short History of Epidemiology for Noninfectious Diseases in Japan, Part 3
sources.note: nationwide nutrition survey of 1945 and postwar nutritional disorders. Scope: Survey design and measured groups must be stated; do not claim it captured every region or marginalized population.

sources.title: Minamata Disease: The History and Measures, Chapter 2
sources.note: 1956 first official report; investigation and delayed causal recognition. Scope: Official government account; later victim-centered scholarship is needed for responsibility, stigma, and lived experience.

sources.title: Conservation of the Water Environment in Japan: History
sources.note: 1958 water-quality laws and their limitations. Scope: Page contains a likely typographical date error elsewhere; use only the clearly supported 1958-law passage and corroborate.

sources.title: Mechanical Engineering Heritage No. 57: Dawn of Japanese Home Electric Appliances
sources.note: washing machine was the only domestic model until 1952; appliance diffusion context. Scope: Heritage objects predate 1945 and were initially rare; do not imply mass household ownership before statistics support it.

sources.title: Sony product milestones: TR-55 transistor radio
sources.note: 1955 TR-55 and 1952 transistor-license decision. Scope: Corporate celebratory source; safe for model/date only, not broad claims of social impact without independent evidence.

sources.title: Nissin Foods Group history: Chicken Ramen
sources.note: August 25, 1958 launch. Scope: Corporate origin story; do not claim immediate universal adoption or repeat superlatives without qualification.

sources.title: 1955 Crown, first generation
sources.note: 1955 first-generation Crown model page. Scope: Corporate model record; car ownership and worker conditions require independent statistics.

sources.title: Fiscal History of Shōwa: From Defeat to the Peace Treaty
sources.note: volumes on prices, wages, budgets, reparations, and occupation reforms. Scope: Use precise volume/chapter locators before inserting figures; official fiscal history privileges state policy.

sources.title: Ground Zero 1945
sources.note: occupation censorship and publication of Hiroshima/Nagasaki images in 1952. Scope: Images of testimony made decades later are retrospective memory, not contemporaneous photographs.

sources.title: When Empire Comes Home: Repatriation and Reintegration in Postwar Japan
sources.note: Introduction and chapters on repatriation, reintegration, and new national identity. Scope: Use route- and group-specific evidence; repatriates from Manchuria, Korea, Sakhalin, Taiwan, and elsewhere had different experiences.

sources.title: Embracing Defeat: Japan in the Wake of World War II
sources.note: chapters on shattered lives, black markets, democracy, constitutional reform, imperial responsibility. Scope: Secondary synthesis; verify quotable anecdotes against its notes and avoid letting Tokyo dominate the entire archipelago.

sources.title: Japan's New Middle Class: The Salary Man and His Family in a Tokyo Suburb
sources.note: Mamachi fieldwork, 1958-1960; salaryman household rhythms and aspirations. Scope: Pseudonymous Tokyo suburb and emerging middle class; never present as a universal Japanese household.

sources.title: Policy toward Koreans in Japan and the 1950s repatriation project to North Korea
sources.note: 1952-1959 policy conflict and February 12, 1959 cabinet decision. Scope: Do not describe the program as simple voluntary homecoming; motivations, misinformation, and coercive context require nuance.

sources.title: Tokyo 1955-1970: A New Avant-Garde
sources.note: 1955-1960 artists, photography, graphic design, experimental film, and protest context. Scope: Tokyo-centered and extends beyond 1960; select only works securely dated within the interval.

Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.

Imported border coordinates remain unchanged. Historical events and map coverage are distinguished in prose; see batchIdentityNotes for conflicts.

proposedOverrides.summary: Postwar Japan under Allied occupation to 1952, then sovereign reconstruction to 1960, with the atlas label error disclosed.

batchIdentityNotes: Japan (USA) is an atlas occupation shorthand, not a polity, annexation, citizenship category, or sovereign name.
The U.S.-led Allied occupation ended on April 28, 1952; the atlas id incorrectly persists to its 1960 snapshot.
The exact four-component geometry covers the four main islands at coarse resolution and excludes Okinawa, Amami, Ogasawara, Korea, Taiwan, and southern Sakhalin.
The 1960 switch back to japan-1914 records continuity of the same country, not succession to a new state.
